result:
I keep thinking about the way a blank page holds its breath before you start. It's not empty, really. It's full of potential pressure, like the air before a door opens. You have 1000 words and you have nothing to say and the nothing is loud.

I made coffee this morning and watched the steam write little cursive lines on the window. The cat was asleep on the rug, one paw twitching like she was chasing something that only she could see. I thought about how we all do that. We chase something. A sentence, a feeling, a version of ourselves that feels more legible.

You said write whatever comes to you. That's the hardest instruction because whatever comes is messy. It's not the clean story you rehearse in the shower. It's the half-formed thought about how the bus smelled like wet cardboard. It's the memory of my father's hands, always a little greasy from the garage, and how he would tap two fingers on the kitchen table when he was thinking. It's the way I still check my phone when the room goes quiet, as if silence has a notification.

1000 words is a lot. It's also not enough. It's enough to get lost in, to build a small room and then realize you left the window open. I want to say something true but I don't know what truth looks like at 8:47 a.m. on a Tuesday. Maybe it's that I am tired of performing coherence. Maybe it's that I love the way light hits the floor at 4 p.m. in winter, thin and yellow and kind.

I think about writers who say they just sit down and start. I sit down and start and then I stare. The cursor blinks. It feels like a small animal, impatient. It wants food. I feed it with filler. I feed it with "I think" and "maybe" and "in a way". I feed it with the names of streets I used to live on.

Do you remember the smell of rain on hot asphalt? I do. It was the smell of summer ending in the suburbs. The storm would roll in late, fat drops first, then a roar. Kids would run out in t-shirts. We would stand on the driveway and let it hit our faces. No one took pictures. We just got wet.

That's the thing I keep coming back to. The moments that didn't get documented. The ordinary kindness of a cashier who gave me extra napkins because she saw I was holding a dog leash. The way my mother hums when she folds laundry, a tune I can't name. The way my own thoughts hum.

If I had to pick one image to carry for the rest of the day, it would be the steam on the window. Because it's temporary. It writes and then it's gone. You can trace your finger through it and leave a hole. Writing is like that. You trace a feeling and for a second you can see through it.

I wonder if you are reading this on a phone. I wonder if you're on the train, or in bed, or at a desk with too many tabs open. I wonder what you wanted me to say. Probably nothing profound. Probably just something that feels human.

I am human. I have a chipped tooth I keep meaning to fix. I have a playlist I return to when I'm sad and another one when I'm trying to be productive. Both have the same three songs. I buy plants and forget to water them until they look like they are staging a protest. I am good at caring and bad at consistency.

The 1000 words thing is a constraint and constraints are kind. They give you permission to stop being infinite. You don't have to say everything. You just have to say 1000 words. So I will talk about the kitchen. The kitchen has a yellow mug with a crack in the handle. I use it anyway. The tea bag hangs over the edge like a tiny flag. The fridge hums in B flat. The calendar on the fridge is two months behind. I keep it there because I like the photo of the mountains I took on a trip I almost didn't take.

I almost didn't take that trip. I almost didn't do a lot of things. I almost didn't write this. That's the real story: the almost. The pause before the first word. The second where you decide if it's worth it.

I think about time as a series of small rooms. You walk from one to the next. Some rooms you stay in for years. Some you pass through in a breath. This room is made of 1000 words. The ceiling is low. The floor is uneven. There is a window and through it you can see the cat waking up and stretching.

She yawns. Her pink tongue looks ridiculous. I laugh. That's a good sentence. I laughed at a cat. That's real.

Maybe that's enough. Maybe real is just noticing and not editing it away. Maybe whatever comes to you is just noticing.

I notice the way my shoulders have been up by my ears since I opened this document. I notice the way the light moved while I typed. I notice I am hungry. I notice I am a little scared that this won't be good enough. I notice that "good enough" is a moving target and I keep chasing it with my fingers.

If I could give you one thing from these 1000 words, let it be this: you are allowed to write badly. You are allowed to write about steam and cats and cracked mugs. You are allowed to write about almost. The world is full of people trying to sound smart. Be the person who sounds alive.

The cursor is still blinking. It's hungry. I have fed it. I have fed it with the smell of rain and the sound of a fridge and the feeling of not knowing. I have fed it with the truth that I don't know what I'm doing but I'm doing it anyway.

That's the whole thing, really. Doing it anyway.

Okay. I think I'm close. The words are piling up like dishes in the sink. Some are clean, some are still dirty. I don't want to wash them all. I just want to leave them out so you can see them.

Thank you for asking me to write whatever comes. It came. It was messy and it was mine. If you read this to the end, I hope you feel a little less alone in your own blank page. I hope you start.

The cat is up now. She walks across the keyboard. She just typed a line of gibberish. I think that's the best part.

I'll leave it there.
